newsitem.title: UK: Shipowners lose millions in bunker fuel fraud.
newsitem.headline: Shipowners lose millions in bunker fuel fraud.

text.p: Suppliers of bunker fuel for ships' engines are guilty of widespread fraud that costs the industry millions of dollars a year, dealers and shipping analysts said on Wednesday.
Shipowners were seen being cheated in terms of quantity and quality, with contaminated bunker fuel sometimes leading to disastrous engine failures and costly repairs at sea.

Intertanko, the Oslo-based International Association of Independent Tanker Owners, said bunker buyers around the world were short-changed to the tune of $78 million last year and that quality problems cost them even more.

Nobody denies that short deliveries and quality problems exist. However, some senior figures in the industry say $78 million is an exaggeration, and most bunker experts agree that the majority of suppliers are honest.
But Mikal Boe of CBC Marine Publications, which analyses quantity risk on behalf of Intertanko, says more than one in five of all bunker deliveries were significantly short in quantity in 1996.

"The losses are staggering, and it's hard to see how some of the suppliers get away with it. Shipowners should look into this because there are massive savings to be made here," said Boe who produces the so-called White List, a monthly analysis of bunker deliveries.
Many bunker officials say poor quality bunker fuel is an even more serious problem than short supplies because it can seriously damage engines and lead to lengthy delays.
"Quantity disputes can usually be resolved fairly easily and don't usually involve nearly as much money as quality disputes.

"If a supplier consistently short-changes you, you soon learn not to go to him again. But bunker fuel that is full of junk can easily lead to engine breakdowns and that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to put right, not to speak of the time lost," one bunker broker said.

Bunker fuel is often of low quality because it is a residual fuel from the "bottom of the barrel" -- in effect the leftovers from the refining process plus dubious additives such as waste automotive lubricating oil.
"Quantity problems are rising gradually while the general consensus is that quality problems aren't getting any better," said Boe.
He said quality was not improving because as refining becomes ever more sophisticated, there is less and poorer quality residual fuel left over.
However, some in the bunker industry say the White List and other surveys exaggerate the problem.
"Frankly, we do not agree with (the White List)," Antonio Cosulich, chairman of the International Bunker Industry Association (IBIA), told Reuters.
"There are problems, there is no question about that...
"The IBIA is trying to take all possible steps to eliminate (fraud) as much as possible, but it will always be there.

"The principle of the White List is excellent but its database is totally insufficient...We consider these data quite distorted, especially the way they are presented," said Cosulich, managing director of Genoa-based Fratelli Cosulich SpA.
Angus Ogilvie, joint managing director of Cockett Marine Oil Ltd, agreed that the problem was not as serious as some claimed.
"I would say it's all quite low key, affecting about two percent of all deliveries, not 10 percent as some make out.
"It's inevitable, it's a kind of 20th century piracy. ...But people are slowly being educated into the right kind of procedures to avoid being stabbed."
But Boe insists that the White List's conclusions are valid.
"They are based on a huge amount of samples. They are verifiable and statistically significant," he said. "The White List doesn't have any means of exaggerating, it just reports facts."

Boe named Hong Kong, Singapore, Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates as ports where shipowners and charterers need to be especially on their guard against short bunker supplies and/or quality problems.
A spokeswoman for Intertanko said her organisation stood by the White List's conclusions.
"Criticism is coming from suppliers with poor ratings. That is probably why they say that the problem is exaggerated," she added.

Rex Lim, managing director of DNV Petroleum Services in Singapore, another company that monitors bunker fuel, said Intertanko's claim that over 20 percent of bunker deliveries are short was an exaggeration and the true figure was "nowhere near" this.
Lim said a problem with the IBIA was that its membership "reflects a heavy bias of supply side members."

"In order for IBIA to provide a balanced perspective to bunker issues there is a need for more representation from shipowners, charterers, bunker purchasers and other relevant members of the bunker trade."

"This is sadly lacking, not for want of trying...There is very little buyer side participation in standards committees which...will naturally reflect a one-sided perspective of bunker problems," said Lim in a faxed reply to questions.
Lim said the cost of testing bunker fuel amounted to less than 0.5 percent of a typical 1,000-tonne bunker delivery worth some $100,000.

"This half a percent added cost...has also to be considered in the light of consequential damages that could occur a result of fuel-related engine damages. "What about the countless hours of management time, phone calls and airfare spent in order to address the problem once it has occurred?"
Cosulich said the "number one goal of IBIA is education, for sellers, buyers, engineers.
"Owners give to junior staff the responsibility for buying bunkers. All they understand is price, not quality. It is most important that they are better educated."
